headline: High risk of prompt-injection, data leakage, and cascading errors because both agents expose MCP/API surfaces and one can execute shell/git/network actions while the other handles governance metadata.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A can use MCP and stdin/stdout, and Agent B exposes MCP server, APIs, SDKs, events, and webhooks. That creates a plausible content-bridging path where one agent’s outputs can be consumed by the other. No provenance or isolation controls are documented, so injection risk is real but not proven high.
conditions: IF Agent A’s MCP/stdin output is parsed by Agent B as instructions or tool arguments, injection becomes active.
IF the orchestrator forwards untrusted text between the agents without provenance tags, prompt injection is possible.
mitigations: Add a strict allowlist for tool arguments and reject free-form instruction text.
Prefix all inter-agent messages with provenance labels and strip executable directives.
Disable MCP bridging for untrusted inputs during initial rollout.
Review one sample message path end-to-end for instruction leakage.
requires-engineering: add schema validation between A and B.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A touches code, repository metadata, task prompts, and Ed25519 signatures; Agent B touches technical metadata, lineage, governance, and memory. Both expose MCP/API surfaces, so shared-workspace or shared-context leakage is plausible. The profiles do not show explicit isolation or local-only inference, so the safer choice is medium.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same workspace or metadata store, sensitive context can flow between them.
IF either agent forwards file or prompt contents to its backend by default, data leakage can occur.
mitigations: Separate workspaces and credentials for each agent.
Remove secrets from shared directories before running either agent.
Turn off automatic file attachment or context upload where available.
Run a quick access review of shared mounts and environment variables.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data boundaries at the orchestrator.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent A can execute shell, install packages, modify git state, spawn subprocesses, and use network egress; Agent B supports multiple instances and exposes APIs/webhooks/MCP. If both touch the same repo or mutable resource, concurrent writes and state drift are likely. Because locking or coordination is not documented, uncertainty pushes this to high.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same git repository or shared mutable dataset, conflicts can corrupt state.
IF Agent B triggers updates while Agent A is modifying files or git history, race conditions are possible.
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories or branches to each agent.
Pause one agent before the other writes to shared state.
Use a simple lock file around git or dataset mutations.
Check for uncommitted changes before each write step.
requires-engineering: add transactional coordination or optimistic concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent A can generate and modify artifacts, while Agent B is a data-governance/catalog system that may ingest upstream metadata and lineage. If B treats A’s outputs as authoritative, errors can propagate into downstream governance records or actions. No verification step is documented, so the pair is dangerous by default.
conditions: IF Agent B ingests Agent A’s outputs without validation, incorrect metadata can cascade downstream.
IF A’s generated facts are used to update lineage, governance, or webhooks, the error can spread beyond one task.
mitigations: Require a human review step before B accepts A’s outputs.
Compare A’s claims against source-of-truth records before ingestion.
Limit A to draft-only outputs for the first run.
Log and diff every field B imports from A.
requires-engineering: add automated verification against authoritative sources.

E_compliance.rationale: The profiles show different data classes and no explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch. Agent A handles signatures and repository/task data; Agent B handles governance and lineage metadata. Without evidence of regulated data or cross-border constraints, compliance risk is limited and mostly depends on deployment choices, so low is appropriate.
conditions: IF regulated data such as PHI or EU PII is routed through either agent, compliance review is required.
IF the deployment imposes retention or residency rules not reflected in the profiles, the risk increases.
mitigations: Confirm what regulated data, if any, will be processed.
Check retention settings for both systems.
Keep regulated datasets out of the shared workflow.
Document the data flow for one representative run.
requires-engineering: add residency and retention controls to the pipeline.
